reader_notes: Minor friction (the one place I tripped): Fearnbeck's journal objection asserts that 'celled or not, the flags must still be laid on a bedding course of sand', but the remedy applied to the five failed streets is 'a thin mortar bed drawn up to Fearnbeck's own specification' - i.e. not sand. It is recoverable (his 'must' can be read as 'under current practice'), but a careful reader notices his own prescription contradicts the premise of his argument.

Related unexplored implication: if a thin mortar bed denies the roots the bedding habitat, the text never addresses why mortar-bedding alone would not be the cheap universal fix, which would undercut the case for the four-times-more-expensive cells. Not an error, but a sharp student may ask it.

Q1 distractor C ('bare of living root') sits close to the passage's 'there was almost nothing alive'. The distinction is absolute vs near-absolute wording, and C also concerns the negative finding rather than the located source of the lift. Solvable and defensibly wrong, but it is the tightest call in the set.

Q3's key depends on two inferences chained together: only the five streets had their flags lifted, so the ground under the twenty-five was never examined, reinforced by the closing 'We are reading the flags, not the roots.' Well supported, but it is the most inferential item here. Option C is a good trap because it is exactly the hypothesis the writer refuses to confirm.

Internal arithmetic and chronology check out: 25 within tolerance + 1 spoiled by the water-main trench + 5 failures = the 31 rebuilt streets; and 'seven years ... surveyed every April' is consistent with 'the oldest celled pavement is now in its eighth year'.

The underlying science reads as sound rather than invented: root mats concentrating in the moist, aerated horizon immediately beneath slabs, and load-bearing structural soil crates that keep the loam inside uncompacted, both match real practice. Nothing in the passage felt factually wrong to me.

Q4 is well anchored by the explicit verdict sentence ('On the five streets Fearnbeck's case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not'), so option D (no side taken) is cleanly excluded despite the hedging in the final paragraph.

The invented surnames (Askerholt, Fearnbeck, Welbrace) read as constructed rather than as ordinary British names, but they do not impede comprehension and the register is otherwise convincing broadsheet feature prose.
